claims.text: CPA-based quantum-mechanical simulations incorporating disorder and defect scattering will predict transport properties of HfNbTaTiZr more accurately than analytical models that assume perfect, defect-free crystals.
The predicted accuracy advantage will apply across the nearly 0–200 K and 300–1200 K temperature regimes.
The CPA-based approach will be especially advantageous for HfNbTaTiZr specimens containing 1 wt.% oxygen.
The initial bulk HfNbTaTiZr material can be represented as a disordered solid with typical microstructural features.
A comparison specimen contains 1 wt.% oxygen in addition to HfNbTaTiZr.
CPA-based simulations can capture intrinsic random-alloy disorder and oxygen-induced defect scattering in electronic and thermal transport.
The high-temperature 300–1200 K regime specifically concerns a specimen containing 1 wt.% oxygen.
Atomic-scale alloy disorder and oxygen-related defects scatter charge carriers and phonons.
CPA integrates quantum-mechanical scattering from random alloy disorder and oxygen-induced defects.
Accounting for these non-idealities will improve agreement between simulated and measured electrical and thermal conductivities.
The CPA-based approach will capture enhanced scattering at low temperatures.
The CPA-based approach will capture additional high-temperature resistivity contributions associated with 1 wt.% oxygen.
Existing analytical predictions used as the baseline assume perfect, defect-free crystalline behavior.
The proposed applicability is limited to HfNbTaTiZr between 0–200 K and 300–1200 K and to specimens with or without 1 wt.% oxygen.
Microstructural variation, unmodeled defect types, and grain boundaries may alter the magnitude of the accuracy improvement.
Failure to achieve statistically significant improvement over defect-free analytical models would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The conditions associate the 1 wt.% oxygen specimen specifically with the 300–1200 K regime, whereas the boundary and experiment test oxygen-containing and oxygen-free specimens across both temperature regimes.
